title: 'We're never going to come home': Artemis II commander recalls the most terrifying moment of his 10-day trip around the moon

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A student and a career advisor discuss space-industry internships.

script.en: Professor Lin, I'm torn between two summer internships and I'd value your perspective.
Glad to help. Which two are competing for your attention?
One is with a private firm that builds lunar rovers; the other is with a university lab analysing satellite images of the Moon.
Both sound relevant. What matters most to you this summer?
Honestly, I want something that will strengthen my graduate applications, but I also need to earn enough to cover rent.
That's a practical concern. The private firm pays well, I assume, but does it offer meaningful research tasks?
They said interns mostly handle routine data entry and logistics. The lab, by contrast, would let me join a team mapping lunar craters.
So one offers money, the other offers intellectual engagement. Have you asked whether the lab can provide a stipend?
I haven't. I assumed university labs never pay.
That's a common misconception. Many grant-funded projects include student support. It's worth an email before you decide.
If the lab could offer even a modest stipend, I'd lean toward it.
And don't overlook the network. The lab's director collaborates with NASA on mission planning, which could open doors later.
That's a good point. The firm's prestige is mainly commercial, not scientific.
Exactly. Prestige fades; skills and contacts endure. But make the choice yourself, not because I pushed you.
Understood. I'll contact the lab this afternoon and ask about funding and duties.
Good. And keep the firm as a fallback. A paid backup is never a bad thing.
Thank you. I feel much clearer about how to proceed.

script.en: When a spacecraft travels farther from Earth than any human has gone before, the public tends to focus on the heroic astronauts who ride it into the unknown. Yet the success of such a mission depends just as heavily on the engineers and flight controllers who remain on the ground, monitoring every parameter from a distance. During a recent lunar voyage, the crew commander described a moment of genuine fear: the onboard distance counter kept rising past the planned turning point. For several minutes he believed the craft might never return. In fact, the excess distance was a normal result of orbital mechanics, and the counter soon began to fall as the trajectory unfolded exactly as designed. What makes this anecdote instructive is not the danger itself but the division of labour it reveals so clearly. While the commander watched the numbers with mounting alarm, his crewmates were calmly conducting scientific observations and reporting to mission control. The ground teams, meanwhile, were monitoring the same data and knew the trajectory was proceeding as designed, so they felt no alarm at all. The astronauts' anxiety was real, but it was not shared by those with the fullest picture. This gap between cockpit perception and ground-level knowledge is common in high-risk enterprises, where those closest to the action often see only part of the story. It suggests that effective space missions need not only technical precision but also clear communication between those in the field and those at headquarters. Had the commander been briefed more thoroughly on expected fluctuations, his fear might have been avoided. The episode thus offers a lesson for any organisation managing complex operations: experts in the field may lack the context that specialists at headquarters possess, and bridging that gap is essential.

sections.title: Fear at the Farthest Point
sections.passage: When Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman addressed the Starmus VIII festival, he did not begin with triumph or with the customary celebration of a mission accomplished. Instead, he recalled the moment during his ten-day lunar mission when genuine fear took hold of him, a moment that few in the audience could have anticipated. The crew had been told their maximum distance from Earth would be 219,667 nautical miles, a record for human spaceflight. As the spacecraft shot past that figure and the odometer kept climbing, Wiseman became convinced that something had gone catastrophically wrong. His alarm was understandable, given the circumstances in which the crew was operating. Mission control had assured the crew that 219,667 nautical miles marked the farthest point of their journey, after which they would turn homeward. Yet three minutes after the counter reached that number, it displayed 219,668, and soon 219,669. To Wiseman, each additional mile suggested that the craft had overshot its intended path and might never return. "That was the moment that I felt real fear," he later told the audience. What makes the episode striking is how isolated his panic was, even within the confined space of the spacecraft. While Wiseman fixated on the rising figures, his crewmates were otherwise engaged: two astronauts were conducting scientific observations at the window, and a third was relaying reports to mission control. None of them noticed his private terror, and the ground teams, for their part, were monitoring the same data and understood that the trajectory was proceeding exactly as planned. Eventually the counter began to fall, and Wiseman's dread dissolved into relief. When the odometer clicked back to 219,668, he announced, "We're going home," and the crew cheered. Looking back, he attributed the mission's safe return not to the astronauts but to the engineers and flight controllers on Earth, calling them "the true heroes" whose courage and rigour made the voyage possible. The Artemis II flight, launched on April 1, was the first crewed journey to the Moon since Apollo 17 in 1972, and nearly every moment aboard was livestreamed to a fascinated public. The crew later received the Stephen Hawking Medal for Science Communication. Yet the most instructive aspect of Wiseman's account may be its lesson about perception: those closest to an event may lack the context that specialists elsewhere possess, and bridging that gap is essential in any high-stakes operation.

They were unaware of the rising distance counter.

briefly glanced

long_sentences.en: "I was watching this number, and I saw it hit 219,667, and I thought, 'Great, this is the farthest we will be from Earth, and the next number I will see will be 219,666 ‪—‬ we'll be going home.' But about three minutes later, I didn't see 219,666; I saw 219,668.

Commander Reid Wiseman and his three crewmates were supposed to reach 219,667 nautical miles (252,788 standard miles, or 406,823 kilometers) — farther than any humans have ever traveled from their home planet — before turning back toward Earth on the sixth day of their 10-day mission to the moon.

'Huh? That's weird.' "And then about three minutes later, it goes to 219,669, and that was the moment that I felt real fear because I thought we had just gone too far ‪—‬ we're never going to come home ‪—‬ and so I was very scared," he added.
